A whole city came out to see Jesus. He picked the one man they hated most, and invited himself to dinner.
Luke, chapter nineteen.
Jericho. The last stop on the road up to Jerusalem.
An oasis of palms and balsam, on the pilgrim highway.
The chief tax man here was Zuh-kee-us.
Chief among the publicans. A title found nowhere else in the New Testament.
And he was rich.
Tax men worked for Rome, and kept whatever they squeezed out above the sum.
To his own people, he was a traitor and a thief.
Now Jesus is passing through. Zuh-kee-us can't see over the crowd. For he was little of stature.
So the richest man in town ran ahead, and climbed a sycomore tree.
And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up.
And called him by name.
Zuh-kee-us, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.
Nobody had introduced them.
And the crowd murmured: he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner.
In that world, to eat at a man's table was to stand with him.
But Zuh-kee-us stood up.
Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor.
And if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
Fourfold. Why that number?
The Law of Moses asked a man who confessed a wrong to repay it, plus a fifth.
Fourfold was the penalty for a thief who stole a sheep and sold it.
Zuh-kee-us didn't wait to be caught. He sentenced himself as a thief.
And Jesus said: This day is salvation come to this house, forasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
The crowd called him a sinner. Jesus called him a son of Abraham.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
Pilgrims in Jericho are still shown an old sycamore they call his.
From Jericho, the road climbs to Jerusalem. Within days, Jesus would hang between two thieves.
And he would save one of them, too.
